messages.subject: gl.report.heterozygosity na.rm bug found
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I think I found a mistake in gl.report.heterozygosity with the position of one of the na.rm arguments. Currnetly it doesnt remove missing data when calculating mean heterozygosity per locus with colMeans(), only when averaging across loci with mean(). Therefore it will only remove loci for which there are read errors for all indivudals (highly unlikley) but not NAs 'peppered' through dataset.

See comments below.

 function (gl)  {
  x <- gl
  sgl <- seppop(x)
  hs <- data.frame(lapply(sgl, function(x) mean(colMeans(as.matrix(x,
                                                                   na.rm = TRUE) == 1), na.rm = TRUE)))  ##   should be arg for colMeans() i.e: na.rm = TRUE) == 1, na.rm = TRUE))))

  sums <- data.frame(lapply(sgl, function(x) mean(colSums(as.matrix(x,
                                                                    na.rm = TRUE) == 1), na.rm = TRUE))) ##  and here
  n <- t(sums/hs)
  n <- cbind(row.names(n), n)
  d1 <- data.frame(names = names(hs), hs = as.numeric(hs[1,
                                                         ]))
  d2 <- data.frame(n)
  names(d2) <- c("names", "freq")
  dd <- join(d1, d2, by = "names")
  dd <- dd[order(dd$hs), ]
  par(mai = c(2.5, 1, 0.5, 0.2))
  barplot(dd$hs, names.arg = paste(dd$names, dd$freq, sep = " | "),
          las = 2, cex.names = 1, space = 0, border = F, col = rainbow(nrow(dd)),
          main = "Observed Heterozygosity")
  return(dd)
}

You will also need to fix up how n is calculated or displayed in the plot....

Cheers,
Stephanie

messages.subject: gl.basic.stats per population/cohort?
messages.body_plain:
I was just wondering if there's a function that already exists to do this that I couldn't find...as it is my supervisor (Sam Banks, to give him the credit) helped me write a function to do this, but it requires renaming populations as PopTimestep rather than having them in separate "other" slots.

I want the basic diversity metrics not only for the entire dataset, but for each population over each timestep ( Pop 1 at time 1,2,3, Pop 2 at time 1,2,3 etc ). This is what we have come up with (on genlight data) but it's a bit clunky...I was hoping there was a wrapper that did something similar.

pop_basicstats1 <- function(x) {
  singlepop <- gl.keep.pop(dat, x)
  Hs_singlepop <- gl.Hs(singlepop)
  Ho_singlepop <- gl.Ho(singlepop)
  Fis_singlepop <- (Hs_singlepop - Ho_singlepop)/Hs_singlepop
  return(as.data.frame( rbind (x, mean(Hs_singlepop), mean(Ho_singlepop), mean(Fis_singlepop))))
}

unique(gl.data.filt@pop) # to get the order the results will be given in
all <- lapply(as.list(unique(gl.data.filt@pop)), pop_basicstats1)
all

alldf <- as.data.frame(lapply(as.list(unique(gl.data.filt@pop)), pop_basicstats1)) # this is a really suboptimal way to display the data
alldf

Thanks,
Britt

On Friday, 6 December 2019 09:22:50 UTC+8, Arthur Georges wrote:
> Further to our previous announcement on the upgrade, we would like to elaborate:
>
>
> (a) dartR has been upgraded to accommodate SilicoDArT data, that is, the presence or absence of sequence tags called or not called, as well as the SNP genotype data. There are analyses that cannot be done on tag P/A data, and the scripts trap that. Both forms of data are stored as genlight objects (read in by gl.read.dart and gl.read.silicodart respectively), the distinction being whether the ploidy is 2 (SNP data) or ploidy is 1 (Tag P/A data).
>
> (b) A computational efficiency has been built in to avoid recalculating stats unnecessarily, which is embedded in the genlight objects. This may require you to run gl <- gl.compatability.check(gl) to avoid throwing errors.
>
> (c) The pcoa scripts have been substantially rewritten to distinguish between PCA (SNP or SilicoDArT data as input, covariance matrix based computations) and PCoA (distance matrix input, any distance measure pretty much). Distortions that may arise (manifested as negative eigenvalues in the noise dimensions) from using a sparse matrix (lots of NAs) or non-metric distance measures can be accommodated by applying recognised transformations (sensu ape).
>
> (d) The scripts for fixed differences have been amended to allow greater control and more diagnostics (using gl.collapse repeatedly), though gl.collapse.recursive still works.
>
> (e) A novel approach to standardizing heterozygosity across species and studies has been introduced. Not a panacea, but worth examination. Use gl.report.secondaries to estimate the number of sequence tags with no snps, and use this value in gl.report.heterozygosity (as n.invariant).
>
> There have been some bug fixes, but software development has a problem of reaching a steady state where bugs are removed but new bugs are created at the same rate. Hence the beta release.
>
> Please pipe up with issues.
>
> install.packages("leaflet.providers")
> install.packages("lifecycle")
> install.packages("farver")
> install_github("green-striped-gecko/dartR", ref="dev") # no need to upgrade prior installs, answer no.
>
> A

messages.subject: Re: New Beta version of dartR
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rachel,

Our current script is essentially a wrapper for glPCA of package adegenet, so you would need to look there for the definitive statement. However, I am sure that the genetic distance is the Euclidean distance, which differs by a small constant factor from classical Roger's D. This distance is chosen because, in the absence of missing values, the distances between your individuals can be represented accurately in Cartesian space of sufficient dimension. That is, your data define a space that is both metric and rigidly linear (there is some technical word for this).

In the presence of missing values, the metricity is broken (leading potentially to negative eigenvalues) but this level of distortion is typically negligible, and orders of magnitude lower than the distortion arising from choosing only 2 or 3 dimensions for the representation.

The latest scripls will provide diagnostics for the impact of non-metricity and allow any distance matrix to be provided, finally justifying the name gl.pcoa.

Hope that helps.

A

messages.subject: New Phylogeny Software
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Hope you are all coping with the virus, the lockdowns and the mixed messages we are getting from our leaders depending on which country you are in.

I would like to bring to your attention a new item of software for generating phylogenetic trees from SNP data. This has been a problematic area as many of you would know having been in heated debate with editors and reviewers. Basically,

(a) Distance measures such as those offered by Phylip are contentious and out of vogue even though we now have the computational power to bootstrap them;
(b) Generating phylogenies by concatenating sequence tags and using ML have been debunked by many, with evidence, including Adam Leache. Some editors flatly refuse to entertain these because they do not deal with the species tree, gene tree issues adequately. One said "I would rather see a phenogram!!!"
(c) Packages like Austal II that generate trees for each sequence tag then form a consensus struggle to deal with the noise when the sequence tags are only between 20 and 69 bp, most with a single SNP.
(d) SVD quartets deals with the species tree-gene tree issue appropriately, and has been considered by some to be the best choice, but it does not give branch lengths.
(e) SNAPP is recommended by many, but computational limitations means that you can only include a couple of individuals per population, and so you have to toss a LOT of data.

The authors of SNAPP have now developed a new package called Snapper, which overcomes the limitations of SNAPP by using, if I understand it correctly, allele profiles of populations rather than individual genotypes. So instead of trying to deal with 1035 individuals, the algorithm just has to deal with 35 populations.

You might like to give it a try.

Stoltz,M, Bauemer, B., Bouckaert, R., Fox, C., Hiscott, G. and Bryant, D. Bayesian inference of species trees using diffusion models. https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.07276.

The software is open-source and available to download athttps://github.com/rbouckaert/snapper <http://github.com/rbouckaert/snapper>.

I expect that the gl2snapp() script in dartR will produce the input file that you pass to BEAUTI to create the xlm file to then pass to Snapper, but I have not tried this.

If you have the time to give this a try, post how you go against this thread, and we can make any mods to the dartR scripts as required.

All the best,

A

Hi Soraia,
Did you get anywhere with this?
I'm was wondering the same thing re which measures were used for calculating beta indicies.
Also Im not 100% sure what the values in the top half of the matricies are... are the beta measures directional or are they some sort of error value?
About to start digging through the source code to figure it out but was hoping you might be able to save me the trouble.
Cheers,
Stephanie

On Tuesday, September 10, 2019 at 8:13:39 PM UTC+10, Soraia Barbosa wrote:
> Hi everyone,
>
> Thank you for developing what it's looking like a very comprehensive and integrative R package!
> I have some questions regarding the interpretation of results from gl.diversity, which might just relate to my lack of understanding of the functions.
>
> I calculated alpha and beta diversity for q=0, q=1 and q=2, and I'm now trying to interpret the data based on what is described in Sherwin et al. 2017.
> I understand that for within population diversity, i.e. alpha values, q=0 represents allelic richness index, q=1 Shannon information index and q=2 heterozygosity index, and that these indices are represented by H values. These H values can then be converted to a common scale of effective numbers, D.
> For between population comparisons of diversity, i.e. beta values, q=0 represents number of allelic types not shared between pops, q=1 measures the chance of a type of individuals providing info on the sampling locality, and q=2 measured the chance of two random individuals from different localities having different allelic types.
> Please correct any of these if I'm wrong.
>
> My question with beta diversity is that the supp material of Sherwin et al. 2017 provides many options to calculate each of these indices, and I'm not sure what the output from gl.diversity represents for each index. For example, Beta diversity for q=1 can represent the Mutual Information (I) or Shannon differentiation, but I'm not sure what is outputted. Do we get only calculations of H and D and we then need to calculate these measures a posteriori with a different function? Can we interpret H and D directly for both alpha and beta?
>
> Any guidance would be most welcome.
>
> Best,
> Soraia

messages.subject: Re: New Beta version of dartR
messages.body_plain:
Hello Dr. Georges,

I am having some troubles that I attribute to the update of the package, but I might be wrong....
The thing is, after the update, my script doesn't run in the same.
For example:

> gl.report.callrate(liza)
Starting gl.report.callrate
  Processing a SNP dataset
Error in !x@other$loc.metrics.flags$monomorphs : invalid argument type

and when I run the command

gl.plot(liza, col=c("DeepSkyBlue", "DeepPink1", "Gold"), legend = F)

It doesn't recognize the colours or the command not to show the legend

But I had run this script a thousand times before....
What I am doing wrong?

Thank you!

Em quinta-feira, 5 de dezembro de 2019 22:22:50 UTC-3, Arthur Georges escreveu:
> Further to our previous announcement on the upgrade, we would like to elaborate:
>
>
> (a) dartR has been upgraded to accommodate SilicoDArT data, that is, the presence or absence of sequence tags called or not called, as well as the SNP genotype data. There are analyses that cannot be done on tag P/A data, and the scripts trap that. Both forms of data are stored as genlight objects (read in by gl.read.dart and gl.read.silicodart respectively), the distinction being whether the ploidy is 2 (SNP data) or ploidy is 1 (Tag P/A data).
>
> (b) A computational efficiency has been built in to avoid recalculating stats unnecessarily, which is embedded in the genlight objects. This may require you to run gl <- gl.compatability.check(gl) to avoid throwing errors.
>
> (c) The pcoa scripts have been substantially rewritten to distinguish between PCA (SNP or SilicoDArT data as input, covariance matrix based computations) and PCoA (distance matrix input, any distance measure pretty much). Distortions that may arise (manifested as negative eigenvalues in the noise dimensions) from using a sparse matrix (lots of NAs) or non-metric distance measures can be accommodated by applying recognised transformations (sensu ape).
>
> (d) The scripts for fixed differences have been amended to allow greater control and more diagnostics (using gl.collapse repeatedly), though gl.collapse.recursive still works.
>
> (e) A novel approach to standardizing heterozygosity across species and studies has been introduced. Not a panacea, but worth examination. Use gl.report.secondaries to estimate the number of sequence tags with no snps, and use this value in gl.report.heterozygosity (as n.invariant).
>
> There have been some bug fixes, but software development has a problem of reaching a steady state where bugs are removed but new bugs are created at the same rate. Hence the beta release.
>
> Please pipe up with issues.
>
> install.packages("leaflet.providers")
> install.packages("lifecycle")
> install.packages("farver")
> install_github("green-striped-gecko/dartR", ref="dev") # no need to upgrade prior installs, answer no.
>
> A
